title: Family Health Behaviors
research_question: How do severe health events experienced by one member of a family or social network causally shape the health-related behaviors and preventive care consumption of other family members and peers? Through what channels—such as learning new information about one's own health risks versus heightened salience of health—do these spillovers operate, and how far do they extend across spouses, adult children, in-laws, and coworkers?
data_description: The study uses Danish administrative register data covering the entire adult population from 1980 to 2011. Health utilization data come from three sources: the Prescription Drug Database (1995-2011) with detailed ATC medication codes; the Health Insurance Registry (1985-2011) covering primary care and specialist contacts; and the National Patient Registry covering inpatient hospitalizations (1980-2011) and outpatient visits (1994-2011) with ICD diagnosis codes. Family health events and timing are identified using hospitalization records and the Cause of Death Registry (from 1980). Demographics (age, gender, education) and employer-employee linkages come from the Integrated Database for Labor Market Research. The unit of observation is the household-year. Key outcomes include statin consumption, cholesterol blood tests, smoking-cessation medication, opioid daily doses, diagnostic radiology expenditures, and hospital contacts. Monetary values are in 2000 Danish kroner.
institutional_context: The setting is Denmark, which provides near-universal and comprehensive public health insurance, removing coverage availability as a confounder for health care utilization decisions. The analysis centers on sudden, severe health events—first-time nonfatal heart attacks and strokes—which are widely viewed as having unpredictable timing and are directly linked to a well-defined preventive treatment (cholesterol-lowering statins, among the most prescribed medications globally). A complementary setting examines fatal events of various causes, including cardiovascular disease and cancers, where survivors' behavioral responses (smoking cessation, opioid use, cancer screening via diagnostic radiology) can be studied. Rich administrative linkages allow tracing impacts across multiple network circles: spouses and cohabiting partners, adult children, sons- and daughters-in-law, and coworkers within the same physical workplace establishment, distinguished by occupation class and age proximity.
ground_truth_notes: The study uses a quasi-experimental design with potential randomness in shock timing, but there may still be unobserved factors affecting the results.

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.identification_strategy: One-line: EVENT_STUDY — treatment = households experiencing a health shock in year τ, control = households experiencing the same shock but in year τ + Δ; shock/instrument/cutoff = severe health shocks (nonfatal heart attacks and strokes)

key_variables.treatment: households experiencing a health shock in year τ
key_variables.control: households experiencing the same shock but in year τ + Δ
key_variables.outcome: consumption of preventive care and health-related behaviors
key_variables.instrument_or_cutoff: severe health shocks (nonfatal heart attacks and strokes)

_legacy_v1_ground_truth.conclusion_detail: Spouses and adult children immediately improve their health behaviors in response to health shocks, with effects being significant and persistent.
_legacy_v1_ground_truth.main_effect: 15% increase among prime-age spouses, 37% and 16% increases among younger and older adult children respectively
key_robustness: alternative control group matching on pre-shock risk factors
